questions.question: Define Economics, name the four factors of production with their rewards, and list the three processes of economic activity.
questions.expected_answer: Economics is the social science that studies how individuals, businesses and governments use limited resources to satisfy unlimited needs and wants. The four factors and rewards, always in pairs: natural resources earn rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit. The three processes in working order: production (combining factors to create goods and services), exchange (trading them through markets and money) and consumption (using them to satisfy wants — which then refill). Every economy, from a driveway car wash to the whole country, runs all three.

questions.question: Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics with an example of each, and sort a positive statement from a normative one.
questions.expected_answer: Microeconomics studies individual units — one household, one firm, one market: why the salon raised the price of braids, why a shop hires an extra driver. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, national unemployment, total output: the cost of living, national growth. Test: can you point at it from your gate (micro) or does it need the whole country in frame (macro)? Positive statements measure and can be tested — 'bus fare rose by two rand'; normative statements judge what ought to be — 'the fuel levy should be scrapped'. Label the sentence before arguing about it.

questions.question: Describe the scientific method economists use, explain ceteris paribus, and argue why Economics is a science that must stay humble.
questions.expected_answer: The loop: observation (data on prices, jobs, spending — Stats SA, the Reserve Bank), hypothesis (a proposed explanation), testing (against statistics and history, since whole economies cannot be rerun in a lab), and law or theory for what survives. Ceteris paribus — all other things equal — isolates one relationship while everything else is held still in thought, because in reality everything moves at once. Economics uses scientific method — empirical, quantitative, model-building — but studies people, who learn and react to predictions about themselves (stocking up before an announced petrol increase). So its laws are tendencies, its forecasts carry error, and disagreement between economists is normal science on difficult material.
